rationale: The strongest alternative is that righteousness is a broader, context-sensitive category of rightness before God: sometimes conduct conforming to God’s will, sometimes a forensic standing granted by grace, and sometimes God’s own justice or covenant faithfulness. That alternative properly cautions against making commandment-doing the exhaustive lexical meaning in every passage, but it does not explain the book’s central evidence better. Deuteronomy 6:25 directly calls observing the commandments “our righteousness”; Psalm 119:172 identifies the commandments themselves as righteousness; 1 John 3:7 makes doing righteousness constitutive evidence of being righteous; and Revelation 19:8 explicitly identifies the wedding linen as the saints’ plural righteous acts. Together these texts strongly establish the book’s distinguishing core: righteousness, particularly as the garment worn by the saints, includes enacted obedience and cannot be reduced to a verdict lacking righteous life. The counter-reading remains useful as a broader semantic framework, especially for Romans, but it subsumes rather than displaces this behavioral core. The chapter’s larger symbolic system and its claim that right-living supplies the substance of every human-righteousness text are less decisively established, so only the core is accepted.
book_core_identification: Human righteousness is enacted right-living under God’s authority—doing what God commands—and therefore cannot be reduced to a forensic verdict received without corresponding righteous conduct; in the garment imagery, this enacted righteousness is what is worn.
book_secondary_elaborations: Every human use of righteousness has right-living as its substance, while grace concerns only its source or reception.
The wedding garment in Matthew 22 is specifically identical with the righteous acts named as fine linen in Revelation 19:8.
Righteous acts are woven into a covenant garment that can subsequently be stained, washed, kept, or defiled.
Ezekiel 16 establishes a sequence of covenant covering followed by clothing in righteous acts.
The coats of skins in Genesis 3 required bloodshed and prefigured the Lamb’s provision of the garment.
Jesus’ footwashing symbolizes post-baptism cleansing of the believer’s daily conduct.
Every piece of the armor of God belongs to one uniform scriptural clothing vocabulary culminating in putting on Christ.
The absence of the wedding garment means having no righteous acts at all.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Righteousness denotes rightness according to God’s norm and has several context-dependent forms: ethical obedience in Deuteronomy, Psalms, 1 John, and Revelation 19:8; forensic right standing or acquittal in Romans 3–4 and Philippians 3:9; and God’s own saving justice or faithfulness in other texts. Commandment-keeping is therefore a genuine manifestation of righteousness but not its exhaustive identity.
counter_core_identification: Righteousness is the broader category of rightness before God, which may denote righteous conduct, forensic standing, or God’s own justice depending on context; commandment-doing is one major instance rather than the universal definition.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that enacted commandment-obedience supplies the necessary substance of every instance of human righteousness, especially passages where righteousness is reckoned, granted, or contrasted with righteousness derived from law.
counter_case: Romans 4:3–8 uses accounting language and immediately interprets blessedness through forgiveness and non-imputation of sin, naturally supporting a forensic dimension.
Philippians 3:9 contrasts Paul’s own law-derived righteousness with righteousness from God through faith, emphasizing source and received standing rather than directly defining conduct.
Scripture applies righteousness to God, who does not obey a superior law, demonstrating that commandment-keeping cannot be the term’s unrestricted lexical definition.
The common interpretation already includes ethical righteousness, allowing the three printed references to be read as clear examples of one established sense without making that sense exhaustive.
The book sometimes moves from an explicit identification in one passage, such as Revelation 19:8, to uniform symbolic equations across passages where the connection is not expressly stated.
book_explanatory_advantages: It closely follows the direct conditional syntax of Deuteronomy 6:25: observing and doing the commandments “shall be our righteousness.”
It gives full force to Psalm 119:172, where God’s commandments are themselves called righteousness.
It accounts naturally for 1 John 3:7, which warns against separating being righteous from doing righteousness.
It explains the plural and active force of Revelation 19:8’s dikaiōmata as righteous acts rather than an abstract status.
It integrates the garment imagery with repeated biblical language of putting on, keeping, washing, and defiling garments as features of lived conduct.
It preserves divine initiative because Revelation says the linen was granted, while also preserving the bride’s agency in arraying herself.

The accepted prior findings concerning belief, faith, and love independently support the coherence of treating obedient response as integral to living covenant fidelity rather than an optional sequel.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It better preserves the evident semantic range of righteousness across ethical, forensic, relational, and divine-agent contexts.
It reads the accounting, forgiveness, and non-imputation language of Romans 4 more straightforwardly as involving legal standing.
It avoids requiring every garment, armor, washing, and covering passage to participate in one fully uniform symbolic code.
It distinguishes what the cited passages explicitly establish from the chapter’s more conjectural links, such as identifying footwashing with continuing garment cleansing.
decisive_sources: Deuteronomy 6:25 — observing and doing all God’s commandments is expressly called “our righteousness.”
Psalm 119:172 — all God’s commandments are expressly called righteousness.
1 John 3:7 — the person who does righteousness is righteous, directly opposing a deedless conception.
Revelation 19:8 — the fine linen is explicitly identified as the righteous acts of the saints and is both granted and put on.
Ephesians 2:10 — good works are divinely prepared yet actually walked in, supporting the chapter’s gift-and-performance distinction.
Accepted prior findings on faith and love — living faith and covenant love necessarily take obedient form, supporting the coherence of the book’s core.
unresolved_objections: The evidence does not establish that commandment-doing exhausts the meaning of righteousness in every biblical context.
Romans 4’s reckoning, forgiveness, and non-imputation language retains a genuinely forensic aspect that the book may understate.
Philippians 3:9 may involve more than a contrast of source and wage-claim; it can also distinguish received standing from law-based performance.
Matthew 22 does not itself identify the missing wedding garment with Revelation 19:8’s linen, even though the canonical association is plausible.
The baptismal interpretation of John 13 and several links involving Edenic clothing, covenant covering, and armor go beyond what is necessary to prove the core.
The book’s general rule that symbols must hold uniformly across Scripture risks suppressing local context and ordinary lexical polysemy.
